archetype.name: Playoff Team (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A team that controls play and scores at a top-two rate, but its goaltending has slipped from last year's elite level, so it looks like a good playoff club rather than last season's juggernaut.

report.headline: Elite offense, ordinary goaltending: a good team whose record and margin disagree
report.take:
Colorado arrives at Thanksgiving at 13-7-3, third in the Central behind Minnesota and Dallas, and eighth on the site. The margin says more than the record does. The Avalanche score 3.91 goals a game, second in the league. Their 0.96 Goal Diff / GP ranks third. Their 5-on-5 shares are firmly positive, with a 53.1 xGF % (9th) and a 53 CF % (5th). Yet the standings hold them back. Pts vs Goal Diff sits at -2.8, 28th in the league, which means they have turned a big goal margin into fewer points than it usually buys. Two overtime losses in the last ten games, to Nashville and Ottawa, are part of that.

The real change from last season is in net. In 2025-26 this team went 55-16-11 for 121 points, with a 56.9 xGF % and a league-best offense and defense. Its goalies saved 34.3 goals above expected that year. This year the Goalies GSAx is -3, 23rd. Mackenzie Blackwood has been fine as the starter at .904 and +2 GSAx. Scott Wedgewood's seven starts have cost them, at .883 and -4.4. The skaters are still very good, though not last year's dominant level. The difference between a 121-point team and a 103-point pace (the sheet's projection) lives mostly in the crease.

The numbers hide something in both directions. The 5-on-5 PDO of 103 is high, and with the goalies below expected, that points to hot 5-on-5 shooting. Some of the scoring should cool. The bad luck in close games should also even out, so the two effects partly cancel. One caution: the sheet's all-situations finishing block (a 25% shooting rate and 1.4 shots a game) is built from a roster listing that shows only one forward, Gabriel Landeskog. It is an artifact, not a signal. Landeskog himself has been productive, with 8 goals, 14 points and a .585 xGF %.

The direction is encouraging. October was a 7-6 month despite a strongly positive goal margin. November has been tighter at the back, with goals allowed down to 2.67 a game from 3.08. The last ten games produced a .700 points percentage. This is a team settling in, and if the bounces in one-goal games turn, the record will start to look like the margin.

strengths.title: A top-two offense
strengths.body: Colorado scores 3.91 goals a game, second in the league and well above the league's 3.2. It is backed by positive shot-attempt and expected-goal shares rather than the power play alone, which sits at 23.1%, roughly league average. Some 5-on-5 shooting luck is folded in, but this has been a top-ten offense in every recent season, so the core of it is real.

strengths.title: Drives play at 5-on-5
strengths.body: A 53 CF % (5th) and 53.1 xGF % (9th) mean the Avalanche have the puck and the better chances most nights. These shares have sat between 52% and 57% for five straight seasons, so they are the stable base of this team rather than a hot month.

strengths.title: Penalty kill and tightening defense
strengths.body: The PK at 81.7% is well above the league's 77.2%. Goals against have fallen from 3.08 a game in October to 2.67 in November, and to 2.4 over the last five games. That improvement has come despite below-average goaltending, which suggests the skaters are giving up less.

concerns.title: Goaltending fell off a cliff
concerns.body: Last year's goalies saved 34.3 goals above expected. This year's are at -3, 23rd in the league. Blackwood has been roughly average, and Wedgewood's .883 has been a clear drag. That gap explains most of the slide from last season's dominance, and it will not fix itself unless Blackwood carries more starts or finds last year's level.

concerns.title: 5-on-5 PDO running hot
concerns.body: A 5-on-5 PDO of 103 with below-expected goaltending means the shooters are converting at an unsustainable clip. Expect the scoring rate to drift down toward last season's level of strong but human finishing, which would trim the goal margin.

concerns.title: Points lagging the margin
concerns.body: At -2.8 Pts vs Goal Diff (28th), Colorado has dropped points it should have banked, including two recent overtime losses. This is mostly noise and should improve, but in a division where Minnesota and Dallas are ahead, the points already lost still count.

trend.note: A 7-6 October that undersold the margin gave way to a tighter November, with fewer goals allowed each month. The last ten games ran at a .700 points percentage, above the season rate.

weekAhead.headline: Two home games around a measuring-stick trip to Minnesota
weekAhead.body:
Montréal comes to Denver with a 14-6-4 record, but it is a record propped up by luck. The Canadiens lead the league in Pts vs Goal Diff at 3.4, and their goal margin is a modest 0.25. Their power play converts just 14.3%, 31st in the league. Colorado already beat them 4-1 in Montréal on Nov. 14. San Jose closes the week in Denver and is the softest matchup: a 43.7 xGF % (30th), 30.4 shots allowed a game (31st), and the most points allowed to forwards in the league.

The Friday trip to Minnesota is the real test. The Wild are 17-3-5, second on the site, and allow the fewest goals in the league. They have an A blueline and the league's best goaltending by GSAx at 16.2. That is a bad matchup for an offense whose shooting is already running hot. Taking four of six points would be a solid week; five or more would signal the close-game luck turning.

keyMatchups.title: Offense vs Minnesota's goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Colorado's second-ranked offense meets the league's top defense and the top Goalies GSAx. Minnesota's skaters only break even on shot attempts at a 50 CF %, so the Avalanche should hold the puck. Whether they finish against an A+ goaltending group decides the game.

keyMatchups.title: Montréal's record outrunning its play
keyMatchups.body: The Canadiens' goal margin ranks 13th, yet they lead the league in points beyond what that margin implies. Their power play is among the league's worst, so a disciplined Colorado game takes away little and leaves them needing more close-game luck.

keyMatchups.title: San Jose's porous defense
keyMatchups.body: The Sharks are out-chanced badly at 5-on-5 and give up 30.4 shots a game. Forwards rack up points against them at the league's highest rate, which sets up a big night for Colorado's A-graded forward group.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net, especially in the back-to-back at Minnesota and home to San Jose. Wedgewood's form is the team's biggest weak spot.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation, solid puck possession and a deep scoring attack, has held for five seasons and should keep Colorado comfortably in the playoff picture. Two things should move in opposite directions. The hot 5-on-5 shooting behind a 103 PDO will likely cool, pulling scoring closer to 3.4-3.7 goals a game. The -2.8 Pts vs Goal Diff should drift back toward neutral, recovering points in one-goal and overtime games.

The swing piece is goaltending. If Blackwood holds around his current level and takes the bulk of the starts, a final total of 98-108 points is the right range, with a second or third seed in the Central the most likely outcome. If the crease reverts to last year's form, they push back toward the top of the conference. If Wedgewood keeps getting a third of the starts at his current level, the lower end is in play.
swingFactors: How much the hot 5-on-5 shooting cools
Close-game and overtime luck evening out

confidence.note: 23 games is a fair sample with strong history behind it, but the roster listing is thin and luck stats are volatile.
